questions.question: What is the initial IV dose of dantrolene in suspected malignant hyperthermia?
questions.explanation: Give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated (typically 1 mg/kg boluses) until the hypermetabolic signs settle. A cumulative 10 mg/kg is a common point to reconsider the diagnosis, not a starting dose.

questions.question: Which is typically the earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia under general anaesthesia?
questions.explanation: Hypercarbia (rising EtCO₂ despite increased minute ventilation) and tachycardia appear early. Hyperthermia is often a late sign.

questions.question: In local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), what is the initial bolus of 20% lipid emulsion for an adult?
questions.explanation: Give 1.5 mL/kg of 20% lipid emulsion IV over about 1 minute, then start an infusion (0.25 mL/kg/min in the ASRA checklist). Repeat the bolus if instability persists.

questions.question: In which patient does succinylcholine carry the highest risk of life-threatening hyperkalaemia?
options: Patient with a spinal cord injury 3 weeks ago
questions.explanation: Denervation (spinal cord injury, stroke), burns and prolonged immobilisation cause up-regulation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors, typically from about 24–72 hours after the injury, so succinylcholine can cause a large potassium release.

questions.question: Which neuromuscular blockers can sugammadex reverse? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Sugammadex encapsulates aminosteroid blockers (rocuronium most strongly, then vecuronium). It has no effect on benzylisoquinolinium drugs such as cisatracurium or mivacurium.

questions.question: Approximately what is the MAC of sevoflurane in a 40-year-old adult (in oxygen)?
questions.explanation: Sevoflurane MAC is about 2% at age 40. For comparison: halothane ~0.75%, isoflurane ~1.15%, desflurane ~6%.

questions.question: Nitrous oxide should be avoided in a patient with an undrained pneumothorax.
questions.explanation: N₂O is 30–35 times more soluble in blood than nitrogen, so it diffuses into closed air spaces faster than nitrogen leaves and enlarges them.

questions.question: In the modified Mallampati classification, what is seen in class III?
options: Soft palate, fauces, uvula and pillars
Soft palate and base of the uvula
questions.explanation: Class I: soft palate, fauces, uvula, pillars. Class II: soft palate, fauces, uvula. Class III: soft palate and base of uvula. Class IV: hard palate only.

questions.question: Neostigmine is given with an antimuscarinic such as glycopyrronium to counter its muscarinic side effects.
questions.explanation: Neostigmine raises acetylcholine at muscarinic as well as nicotinic receptors, causing bradycardia, bronchospasm and secretions. Glycopyrronium (or atropine) blocks these effects.

questions.question: What train-of-four ratio (adductor pollicis) indicates adequate recovery from neuromuscular block before extubation?
questions.explanation: A TOF ratio ≥ 0.9 measured quantitatively. Four visible twitches or a subjective absence of fade does not exclude residual block.

questions.question: What is the adult intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) dose for anaphylaxis?
questions.explanation: 0.5 mg IM (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL, i.e. 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed. Under anaesthesia with IV access, experienced anaesthetists titrate IV boluses of 50 µg instead.

questions.question: Which are typical early symptoms of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity? (Select all that apply.)
options: Bradycardia as the first sign in every case
questions.explanation: Early CNS symptoms include perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, light-headedness and agitation. Cardiovascular collapse can occur, sometimes without prodromal CNS signs, but bradycardia is not a universal first sign.

questions.question: Under ASA fasting guidance for elective procedures in healthy patients, what is the minimum fast after a light meal?
questions.explanation: ASA guidance: clear liquids 2 h, breast milk 4 h, infant formula / non-human milk / light meal 6 h; fried or fatty food or meat may need 8 h or more.

questions.question: What is the typical feature of a post-dural puncture headache?
questions.explanation: The headache is postural: it worsens within about 15 minutes of sitting or standing and eases lying flat, typically frontal-occipital, often with neck stiffness.

questions.question: Is ropivacaine an ester or an amide local anaesthetic?
questions.explanation: Amide local anaesthetics have an 'i' in the name before '-caine' (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine). Esters include procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine and cocaine.

questions.question: Volatile anaesthetics inhibit hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in a dose-dependent way.
questions.explanation: Volatile agents attenuate HPV dose-dependently, which can matter during one-lung ventilation; the effect at about 1 MAC is modest.

questions.question:
Interpret this arterial blood gas:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| pH | 7.25 |
| PaCO₂ | 60 mmHg (8.0 kPa) |
| HCO₃⁻ | 26 mmol/L |
questions.explanation: Low pH with high PaCO₂ means respiratory acidosis. Bicarbonate is near normal (acute rise ≈ 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg PaCO₂ above 40), so there has been no time for renal compensation: acute.

questions.question: What is typically the earliest ECG change in hyperkalaemia?
questions.explanation: Peaked T waves come first; then PR prolongation and P-wave flattening, QRS widening and finally a sine-wave pattern, VF or asystole. U waves suggest hypokalaemia.

questions.question: What dexamethasone dose is commonly recommended for PONV prophylaxis in adults, given at induction?
questions.explanation: Consensus guidelines suggest 4–5 mg IV at induction for PONV prophylaxis (8 mg is also used, e.g. when an anti-inflammatory effect is wanted).

questions.question: Which are risk factors in the simplified Apfel score for PONV? (Select all that apply.)
options: History of PONV or motion sickness
questions.explanation: The four Apfel factors are female sex, non-smoking status, history of PONV/motion sickness and postoperative opioids. Risk with 0/1/2/3/4 factors is roughly 10/20/40/60/80%.

questions.question: What rocuronium dose is typically used for rapid sequence induction?
questions.explanation: 1.0–1.2 mg/kg gives intubating conditions in about 60 seconds, comparable to succinylcholine. 0.6 mg/kg is the standard (non-RSI) intubating dose.

questions.question: Naloxone has a longer duration of action than morphine.
questions.explanation: Naloxone's effect lasts roughly 30–90 minutes, often shorter than the opioid it reverses, so respiratory depression can return; repeated doses or an infusion may be needed.

questions.question: In a 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' (CICO) situation, which technique does the 2015 Difficult Airway Society guideline recommend?
questions.explanation: DAS 2015 Plan D: front-of-neck access with a scalpel cricothyroidotomy (scalpel, bougie, size 6.0 cuffed tube), with the patient fully paralysed.

questions.question: This capnography trace shows a sloped, 'shark-fin' upstroke. What is the most likely cause?
options: Rebreathing from an exhausted CO₂ absorber
questions.explanation: Slow expiratory emptying from obstructed airways produces the prolonged, sloped phase II–III upstroke. Oesophageal intubation shows little or no CO₂; rebreathing raises the baseline.
